1oapfy: The form and its first use: what never happened
am1nlc: The conditional perfect is formed with the conditional of «haber» plus the past participle: habría, habrías, habría, habríamos, habríais, habrían + terminado. Its best-known use is to present a past consequence that did not happen. The condition can come with «si + hubiera», but also with a phrase: «con un buen arquitecto», «sin la lluvia», «en tu lugar».
7ejoy5: Don't confuse it with the pluperfect indicative: «la obra había terminado» reports a real earlier fact; «la obra habría terminado» imagines or calculates something that was not confirmed.

878qki: The conditional perfect also moves the future perfect into the past. If in March the builder said «para junio habremos terminado», today we report it like this: «dijo que para junio habrían terminado». Look for the deadline: «para», «antes de», «a fin de mes».
1xv9rpi: It also serves to reproach gently: instead of an impossible order about the past, it describes the expected alternative that wasn't taken. «Habrías podido avisarme» or «habrías debido consultar» point out a failing without attacking. «Tendrías que haber…» and «podrías haber…» have the same value.
1q2ve55: For reference: you will also hear the conditional perfect used for guesses about the past, as in «cuando llegó el camión, habrían sido las diez».

7d6jyf: Original SpanishCue text written as a post on Inés Ortiz's fictional blog. The people, the house and the company are invented.
888adv: Today it is a year since we first slept in the house on Urquiza Street. That day there was no hot water, the kitchen ceiling was dripping and the front windows were two sheets of plastic tied with tape. If someone had shown me a photo of that night when we were living in Buenos Aires, we probably wouldn't be here. Luckily, nobody took one.
1oxnmxh: The renovation taught us a lot, almost always the hard way. The building firm had promised us that in four months they would have finished; they took nine. I understand that a house from 1940 hides surprises, but they could have explained to us from the start that the estimate was optimistic. We, for our part, should have asked for a contract with dates. If we had signed one, today we wouldn't still be arguing about who pays for the pipe that burst in August.
1si52xb: I also learned things about myself. If I were a calmer person, I wouldn't have spent the nights of April looking at photos of kitchens we couldn't afford. Federico, on the other hand, is patient by nature; if he weren't, I think the builder would have walked off the job in May. We divided the roles without saying so: I worried and he negotiated.
rvywhi: The neighbours were another surprise. Doña Rosa, from the house opposite, let us use her bathroom for three weeks without us asking. If we hadn't met her, I don't know how we would have survived September. Today she invites us for mate on Sundays and tells us what the street was like when it wasn't paved. If we were still living in a twelve-storey building, we probably wouldn't even know the name of the neighbour next door.
1n56vk2: What would have happened if we had stayed? I don't know. Maybe I would have got a promotion, maybe not. What I do know is that today I have breakfast in the garden, I cycle to work and on Sundays we look at the river from the riverside walk. If we hadn't made that change, I would still be waiting for the perfect moment to change my life. And that moment, I know now, never comes on its own.
